title: Bombette Pugliesi
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Small, tightly rolled pork bundles from Puglia, stuffed with cheese and cured meat, grilled until the outside chars while the cheese inside turns molten.
longDesc: Bombette, meaning 'little bombs,' are a beloved feature of Puglian butcher shops and grills, thin slices of pork rolled around a simple filling and secured tightly enough to hold together over live fire, bursting with melted cheese at first bite.
ingredients: 8 thin slices pork capocollo or loin, about 80g/3oz each
150 g (1½ cups) caciocavallo or provolone cheese, cut into batons
steps: If needed, gently pound the pork slices to an even thinness.
Lay a slice of pancetta over each pork slice.
Season with garlic, parsley, salt, and pepper, then place a baton of cheese at one end.
Roll each slice up tightly around the cheese, securing with a toothpick to hold its shape.
Brush the rolls with olive oil.
Grill over medium-high heat, turning occasionally, for about 15–20 minutes until the pork is cooked through and nicely charred on the outside.
Let rest for a couple of minutes before removing the toothpicks and serving hot.
chefTips: Roll the bombette tightly so the cheese stays sealed inside rather than leaking out during grilling.
A charcoal grill gives the most authentic smoky char, though a grill pan works well too.
Let the meat rest briefly after cooking so the melted cheese doesn't immediately spill out when cut.
commonMistakes: Rolling too loosely, causing the cheese filling to leak out over the fire.
Overcooking, which can dry out the relatively thin pork slices.
Skipping the securing toothpick, risking the rolls unraveling on the grill.
storage: Best eaten fresh; refrigerate leftovers for up to 2 days.
reheating: Reheat gently in a covered pan or oven.
healthBenefits: A good source of protein from the pork and cheese.
culturalNote: Bombette originated in the Valle d'Itria area of Puglia and remain a fixture of local butcher shops, which often grill them fresh to order for customers.
